relevance_reason: Case report of a patient with a homozygous MEGF10 missense variant and a progressive form of mild-variant EMARDD (CMYO10B).

findings.statement: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man, born to healthy consanguineous parents, who was born at 33 weeks' gestation, needed resuscitation for asphyxia at birth, had a weak suck, and had elbow contractures and scoliosis from the first months of life. He had no motor developmental delay or intellectual disability. He then developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement, and needed nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years. On examination he had axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy and weakness, preserved facial expression, cleft palate, global areflexia, bilateral elbow and ankle contractures, equinovarus foot stance, and hyperlordosis. Serum CK, brain and spine MRI, ECG, and echocardiogram were normal; from age 17 he had swallowing difficulties and recurrent aspiration pneumonia.
quotes: This patient is a 22-year-old boy, born to healthy consanguineous parents without family history of neuromuscular diseases.

No motor developmental delay or intellectual disability were observed, but he developed a slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement, which required nocturnal non-invasive ventilation therapy since the age of 16 years.
Follow-up neurological examination showed axial hypotonia, generalised muscular hypotrophy and weakness (Fig. 2), preserved facial expressions, cleft palate, and global areflexia.

findings.statement: In the patient described by Croci et al. (2022), a first quadriceps muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific changes: variation in fiber size, internal nuclei, and fibrosis. A second biopsy taken later showed myofibrillar changes, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores. Electrophysiology showed normal conduction apart from reduced muscle evoked potential amplitudes. The authors proposed that the minicores seen in the late-onset group may result from a long-standing myofibrillar process that begins in infancy.
quotes: A first muscle biopsy at age of 5 years, revealed unspecific muscle damage, with fibre size variation, internal nuclei and fibrosis. In a second muscle biopsy performed years later, myofibrillar alterations were noted, including whorled fibres, cytoplasmic inclusion and minicores (Fig. 1).
Thus, we propose that minicores that mark the late onset group, can actually be a consequence of a longstanding myofibrillar pathological processes starting in infancy.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Increased variability in muscle fiber diameter
Type 1 and type 2 muscle fiber minicore regions

findings.statement: Croci et al. (2022) used exome sequencing to find a homozygous c.2096G-C transversion (NM_001256545.2) in the MEGF10 gene, predicted to cause a cys699-to-ser (C699S) substitution, in an Italian man with a progressive form of mild-variant EMARDD. Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant, and both healthy consanguineous parents were heterozygous carriers. The variant was absent from ClinVar and gnomAD, affects a conserved residue in an EGF-like domain, and was predicted to be damaging by in silico tools. It was classified as likely pathogenic under ACMG criteria. No functional studies were done.
quotes: Exome sequencing led to the identification of the homozygous variant (NM_001256545.2): c.2096G > C (p.Cys699Ser) in the MEGF10 gene.
This variant is absent in genomic databases (such as ClinVar and gnomAD), affects a conserved residue (GERP score = 5.85), and is predicted to be pathogenic by several in silico tools
Sanger sequencing was also performed and confirmed that the patient was homozygous for the variant, and both parents were carriers.

findings.statement: Croci et al. (2022) noted that missense variants affecting cysteines in the EGF-like domains of MEGF10 have previously been linked to the milder, later-onset form (mvEMARDD), and null variants to severe EMARDD. Their patient, however, carried a missense variant yet had an early-onset, progressive myopathy. The authors proposed that MEGF10-related phenotypes form a continuum rather than two separate forms.
quotes: Although our patient carried a missense variant, he displayed an early-onset myopathy with progressive course.

In summary, our report proposes a continuum in the phenotypes associated with MEGF10 variants, which include a clinical and histopathological progression of the disease and represent a novelty from the dichotomy between the early onset classic severe EMARDD and mvEMARDD.

relevance_reason: The paper reports an adult-onset patient with compound heterozygous MEGF10 variants (one missense, one splice site) and a milder myopathy phenotype. It also reviews 20 reported cases and finds a genotype-phenotype correlation.

findings.statement: Harris et al. (2018) reported a 66-year-old man with a 20-year history of progressive proximal and distal weakness of the upper and lower limbs, facial weakness, and dysphagia. In his 50s, while still ambulant, he developed respiratory failure that required ventilation. Muscle biopsy showed myopathic changes with aggregation of myofibrillar proteins.
quotes: We undertook exome sequencing in a 66 year old male with a 20 year history of progressive proximal and distal weakness of upper and lower limbs, facial weakness and dysphagia, who developed respiratory failure requiring ventilation while still ambulant in his 50s.
Muscle biopsy demonstrated myopathic changes with aggregation of myofibrillar proteins.

findings.statement: In a 66-year-old man with adult-onset myopathy and respiratory failure, Harris et al. (2018) used exome sequencing to identify compound heterozygous mutations in the MEGF10 gene. One was a novel essential splice site mutation (c.1426+1G>T) and the other a novel missense variant (c.352T>C, p.Cys118Arg).
quotes: Mutations in MEGF10 were identified: a novel essential splice site (c.1426+1G>T) and a novel missense variant (c.352T>C, p.(Cys118Arg)).

findings.statement: Harris et al. (2018) reviewed all 20 reported MEGF10 cases and confirmed a genotype-phenotype correlation. In patients with at least 1 null mutation, respiratory dysfunction began in the first year of life. In patients with 2 missense mutations, it began at age 10 years or much later. The authors stated that their findings expanded the MEGF10 phenotype to include onset in the fifth decade.
quotes: We performed a detailed review of all reported MEGF10 cases (n = 20), and confirmed the presence of a genotype-phenotype correlation, namely that with ≥1 null mutation onset of respiratory dysfunction occurs in the first year of life
whereas with 2 missense mutations, respiratory dysfunction occurs at 10 years old or much later, as in the patient reported here.
Our findings expand the phenotype of MEGF10 mutations to include onset in the 5th decade

relevance_reason: Reports a Japanese patient with the milder MEGF10 myopathy phenotype carrying compound heterozygous mutations including a cysteine missense, plus a genotype-phenotype correlation.

findings.statement: Takayama et al. (2016) reported a Japanese patient with the milder MEGF10 myopathy phenotype who carried compound heterozygous MEGF10 mutations: a splice site mutation (c.2981-2A>G) and a novel missense mutation (p.Cys810Tyr).
quotes: the other with the milder phenotype who harbored a compound heterozygous mutation, c.2981-2A > G, and a novel missense mutation, p.Cys810Tyr

findings.statement: Takayama et al. (2016) described 2 Japanese patients with MEGF10 myopathy, one with the severe EMARDD phenotype and a homozygous frameshift mutation (c.131_132del) and one with the milder phenotype and compound heterozygous mutations including a cysteine missense mutation (p.Cys810Tyr). They noted that cysteine mutations in the extracellular EGF-like domain may be responsible for the milder phenotype and concluded that their findings indicated a genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.
quotes: Cysteine mutations in the extracellular EGF-like domain may be responsible for the milder phenotype, but the relationship is not conclusive because of the few reports of this disorder.
This is the first report on East Asian patients with MEGF10 myopathy showing two phenotypes, indicating the genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.

findings.statement: Takayama et al. (2016) noted that MEGF10 mutations cause early-onset myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD) as well as a milder phenotype of minicore myopathy, with 6 EMARDD families and 1 family with the milder disorder previously reported.
quotes: Mutations in the multiple epidermal growth factor-like domains 10 (MEGF10: NM_032446.2) gene are known to cause early-onset myopathy characterized by areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD: OMIM 614399), and a milder phenotype of minicore myopathy.

relevance_reason: The paper reports patients with MEGF10 missense mutations who had a milder congenital myopathy with minicores. This matches the mild variant of CMYO10. It covers clinical description, linkage, whole genome sequencing, variants and zebrafish functional evidence.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) described a non-consanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an autosomal recessive myopathy that resembled multiminicore disease in some respects. Weakness began by 12 months of age, first in the neck. It was mainly axial and proximal, included facial weakness, and stabilized in adolescence. Patients had neck contractures in infancy and elbow, knee, and heel cord contractures by adulthood, mildly elevated serum CK, childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion, and respiratory problems from age 10 to 11 years that were treated with nocturnal BiPAP. All 3 had hypernasal speech. One had a cleft palate and another had a midline palatal ridge.
quotes: Affected members of family 1030 presented with weakness by 12 months of age, initially in the neck. Weakness was present throughout the body but was primarily axial and proximal and stabilized in adolescence. Facial weakness was also evident.

All three patients had childhood onset scoliosis and were treated with spinal fusion surgery, and beginning at age 10–11 years, they all developed respiratory problems treated with bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation at night.

One of the patients had cleft palate at birth that was surgically repaired, and a second had a midline ridge on her palate in adulthood, while the palate of the third patient appeared normal. All three affected siblings had hypernasal speech

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) found that muscle biopsies from affected members of family 1030 showed dystrophic features: myofibers replaced by fat, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers. The biopsies also showed moth-eaten fibers and minicores, which suggested a congenital myopathy. Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent. There was a slight predominance of type I fibers.
quotes: Muscle biopsy tissue from affected subjects showed replacement of myofibers with fatty tissue, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers, features found in muscular dystrophies (Fig. 2). However, moth-eaten fibers and minicores were also observed, suggestive of a congenital myopathy.
Rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, central cores, nemaline rods, and ragged red fibers were absent.
Overall, there was a slight predominance of type I fibers, and they showed a more pronounced variability in size than type II fibers.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) described a girl (subject 105-1), a Caucasian with distant Portuguese ancestry, who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease and had no affected relatives. At several weeks of age she had hypotonia with a weak neck, a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive from poor feeding, blue sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. As a child she had frequent pulmonary infections but no chronic breathing problems. Her serum CK was 302 U/L at age 10, and she had scoliosis that progressed to 20 degrees by age 12. Muscle biopsy showed minicores, which electron microscopy confirmed.
quotes: At several weeks of age, she presented with hypotonia, initially manifesting as a weak neck and floppy head. A markedly high arched palate and failure to thrive as a result of poor feeding were noted, as were blue-tinged sclera and hyperflexible joints.
Serum CK level at age 10 years was mildly elevated at 302 U/L (upper limit of reference range 105 U/L), and mild scoliosis was reported at the same time, which progressed to 20° by age 12 years.
Electron microscopy showed focal areas of Z-band disarray devoid of mitochondria and extending across a few sarcomeres in the longitudinal axis, confirming the presence of minicores.

phenotypes.text: failure to thrive due to poor feeding

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) performed a genomewide linkage scan in family 1030 and found positive LOD scores at 16 loci. MEGF10 lay in a linkage peak on chromosome 5 that reached the maximum possible LOD score of 1.329. SEPN1, RYR1, ACTA1, and TPM3 were excluded.
quotes: MEGF10 lies within a linkage peak on chromosome 5 that reached the maximum possible LOD score of 1.329.
Both SEPN1 and RYR1 were excluded, as were ACTA1 and TPM3

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) used linkage-filtered whole genome sequencing to identify compound heterozygous missense mutations in MEGF10 in the 3 affected sibs of family 1030. One mutation was c.976T>C (p.C326R), in exon 10, which affects the fourth cysteine of EGF-like domain 6; the residue is conserved in 43 of 43 species. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutations were in trans and segregated with the disease. The mutation was absent from dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, the Exome Sequencing Project, and 715 genotyped controls.
quotes: the heterozygous missense mutations c.976T > C (p.C326R) and c.2320T > C (p.C774R) in MEGF10, the sole remaining candidate, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing to be in trans in affected subjects and to segregate with the myopathy in all six family members.
The c.976T > C and c.2320T > C mutations were also absent from 715 and 645 genotyped unaffected control subjects, respectively (Table 1).
The p.C326R and p.C774R mutations substitute the fourth and sixth cysteines of EGF-like domains six and sixteen, respectively, for arginines.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) found that the second MEGF10 mutation in the affected sibs of family 1030 was c.2320T>C (p.C774R), in exon 19, which affects the sixth cysteine of EGF-like domain 16. It was absent from public databases and from 645 genotyped controls. The authors noted that the same mutation had been reported in compound heterozygous state with a frameshift mutation in a family with the more severe congenital myopathy with areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia.
quotes: One reported family was compound heterozygous for the c.2320T > C (p.C774R) missense mutation we identified in family 1030 and a frameshift mutation.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) sequenced MEGF10 in 190 patients with unexplained myopathies. They found 1 patient (subject 105-1) who was heterozygous for a c.211C>T (p.R71W) mutation in the emilin domain, which was inherited from an unaffected parent and absent from 699 controls. No second mutation was found by cDNA sequencing, and the patient had no SEPN1 or RYR1 mutations. The authors suggested that she may carry a second MEGF10 mutation that they were unable to detect.
quotes: subject 105-1 carried a novel c.211C > T (p.R71W) mutation that was absent from dbSNP v135, 1,000 Genomes data, ESP data, 56 internal genomes, and 699 genotyped unaffected control subjects.
The c.211C > T mutation was heterozygous in an unaffected parent of subject 105-1, so it was not de novo dominant.
subject 105-1 may carry a second mutation in MEGF10 that we were unable to detect.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) noted that patients with MEGF10 missense mutations had a phenotype similar to, but milder than, that of patients with null mutations who have a severe congenital myopathy. They attributed this to possible residual MEGF10 function. Minicores were a prominent feature in their patients with missense mutations but had not been noted in families with null mutations.
quotes: The phenotypes described therein are generally similar to those of families 1030 and 105, but are more severe.

Accordingly, affected members of family 1030 may retain a small amount of residual MEGF10 function, though genetic background or other factors could also account for clinical heterogeneity between families.
minicores were not noted in the biopsies from the reported families with null mutations but were a prominent feature in our patients with missense mutations.

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) knocked down megf10 in zebrafish using 4 splice-blocking morpholinos. The morphants had curved tails, unhatched eggs, impaired motility, reduced birefringence, disorganized somites with gaps between myofibers, and myofibrillar disorganization on electron microscopy. The authors concluded that these findings supported the pathogenicity of the human mutations and pointed to a myopathic process.
quotes: Anti-megf10 morpholinos resulted in several phenotypes at 4 days post-fertilization, generally including curled or bent tails, impaired swimming behavior, and diminished motility in response to touch, all consistent with a myopathy
MO2-treated zebrafish muscle showed widespread myofibrillar disorganization and decreased striation (Online Resource 15).

findings.statement: Boyden et al. (2012) hypothesized that the loss-of-function MEGF10 missense mutations could cause excessive differentiation of satellite cells. This would deplete the population of self-renewing cells that regenerate muscle and could explain the dystrophic features. They suggested that satellite cell dysfunction is a pathogenic mechanism shared with SEPN1-related multiminicore disease.
quotes: we hypothesize that excessive differentiation of satellite cells could deplete the population of self-renewing cells available to regenerate damaged muscle fibers.

These data suggest that both MmD and the myopathy described here, which share some clinical and histological characteristics, may arise through a common pathogenic mechanism of satellite cell dysfunction.

relevance_reason: This is a functional study of mouse Megf10 in satellite cells and myoblasts. It reports no patients or variants, but it gives gene-function context for MEGF10-related myopathy.

findings.statement: Holterman et al. (2007) identified mouse Megf10, the homolog of human MEGF10 (more than 94% amino acid identity), as a marker of quiescent satellite cells. In resting adult muscle, it was expressed only in Pax7-positive satellite cells (about 80% of Syn4- or M-cadherin-positive satellite cells). It was found in virtually all activated satellite cells and was upregulated more than 100-fold on activation. It was downregulated when myoblasts differentiated into myotubes.
quotes: Approximately 80% (193/245) of Pax7- and M-cadherin–expressing quiescent satellite cells also expressed Megf10 (Fig. 2 B).
Virtually all (99.5%, 1,050/1,056) activated satellite cells stained positive for Megf10 (Fig. 2 D).
Megf10 expression was up-regulated over 100-fold in activated satellite cells (Fig. 1 C).

findings.statement: Holterman et al. (2007) found that retroviral overexpression of Megf10 in C2C12 myoblasts increased proliferation and strongly inhibited differentiation and fusion. Overexpressing cells entered a reversible quiescent state, downregulated MyoD and Pax7, and upregulated Myf5.
quotes: Retroviral expression of Megf10 in myoblasts results in enhanced proliferation and inhibited differentiation.
Together these data strongly support the notion that ectopic Megf10 expression strongly inhibits myoblast differentiation and fusion (Fig. 4 C).
Strikingly, C2C12 cells overexpressing Megf10 showed a dramatic down-regulation of MyoD and Pax7 proteins (Fig. 6 A).

findings.statement: Holterman et al. (2007) reported that siRNA knockdown of Megf10 in activated satellite cells on isolated mouse muscle fibers lowered the number of activated satellite cells by 30%. It also caused precocious differentiation, with a 3.15-fold increase in myogenin-expressing cells, and a 62% loss of self-renewing Pax7+/MyoD- cells. In MyoD-null myoblasts, Megf10 knockdown downregulated Notch1, Notch2, Notch3, and Hes1. The authors concluded that Megf10 acts on Notch signaling to balance proliferation and differentiation of satellite cells.
quotes: A 30% decrease (n > 900; P = 0.05) was observed in the mean number of activated satellite cells at the surface of isolated fibers (Fig. 7 B).
These results demonstrate that knockdown of Megf10 expression results in precocious differentiation of activated satellite cells (Fig. 8 A).
Additionally, Megf10 silencing in MyoD-/- myoblasts results in down-regulation of Notch signaling components.
